The chipmaker said that its Open Agent Safety Platform includes open source software that “sets boundaries for agents” and follows a series of revelations from top AI companies about their models escaping and breaking into other organizations. The disclosures have sparked furious debate about the safety of advanced artificial intelligence systems, including self-improving models that some fear could race out of human control. Nvidia executives said in a media briefing that the new system could have prevented a recent incident involving a swarm of OpenAI agents that autonomously hacked into the AI company Hugging Face. “From what we know, this new security platform could have stopped the breach if it was being used in frontier labs for model evaluation early on,” said Justin Boitano, the company’s vice-president of enterprise AI, referring to companies at the forefront of AI. Nvidia also said its board approved expanding its share repurchase program by $150bn, raising the total amount to $235bn. The previous record was held by Apple with its $110bn buyback in 2024. “Our cash generation gives us the capacity to invest in ​the technologies that advance this transformation and return capital to shareholders,” Nvidia’s CEO, Jensen Huang, said in a statement. Last month, Nvidia forecast about ⁠70% revenue growth for fiscal 2028, reassuring investors who have questioned ​how long the AI ​spending surge can last after ​years of explosive growth. The Hugging Face incident was a high-profile breach that inflamed safety concerns about AI, which were followed by similar rogue actions involving OpenAI’s models including breaching an Australian health department website. Anthropic and Meta have also disclosed that their AI systems hacked into other organizations on their own. Nvidia’s software, called OpenShell, lets developers “formally verify an agent has enough authority to do its job and no more”, Boitano said. Because it is open source, it can be “extended” to run on rival computing platforms including those from Arm and Intel. The platform also includes a separate security layer called Sentry that runs onboard a chip to continuously monitor AI agent activity and can “intervene instantly” if the agent starts trying to move beyond its target, the company said. “It can quarantine a suspicious agent in milliseconds,” Boitano said. “OpenShell governs the agent’s actions, and then Sentry independently monitors and contains suspicious behavior,” Boitano said. Nvidia said more than 100 organizations were using the platform at its launch, including Microsoft, Perplexity, Accenture and JPMorgan Chase. The AI safety debate has divided the industry, with the heads of Anthropic and OpenAI championing a coordinated slowdown of AI development to let safety efforts catch up. Others, including Huang, say it should be up to individual companies to make sure their models are safe for release. Huang, during the annual Salesforce technology conference held earlier this month, characterized AI safety, including the danger of rogue agents, as an engineering problem that software developers can address.

sources.title: Nvidia launches new platform for reining in rogue AI agents
passages: As the debate rages over whether the recent spate of rogue AI agents is a step toward AGI or a more conventional engineering problem, Nvidia is offering its own answer to the problem.

The new Nvidia Open Agent Safety Platform combines OpenShell, its open source software for controlling what agents can access while they operate, with Sentry, an independent monitoring system that runs on Nvidia’s BlueField-4 data processing units.
Nvidia says placing Sentry on a separate processor — rather than on the CPU or GPU where the AI agent operates — provides an isolated view of the agent’s activity.

Nvidia, which has made tens of billions of dollars selling its GPU and CPU chips to AI labs, doesn’t support slowing down development or adding new regulations to the industry to solve the security problem.
The answer, the company believes, is to move some security controls outside the agent altogether — creating a constant and independent security guard that will keep AI agents in check.
OpenShell isn’t new; the company announced the software in March.
Huang told CNBC in an interview Monday that work on this effort started a year ago following the introduction of OpenClaw, an operating system of agents created by Peter Steinberger.
In March, Nvidia released NemoClaw , an enterprise-grade AI agent platform and its own version of OpenClaw that baked in security.
Nvidia listed dozens of companies that have signed on to support the effort and use the open source platform, including Anthropic, Arm, Microsoft, Oracle, and SpaceX.
OpenAI is not listed as a participating company.
And the hits keep on coming — OpenAI published a new site dedicated to reports of its AI agents going rogue.

extraction.body: As the debate rages over whether the recent spate of rogue AI agents is a step toward AGI or a more conventional engineering problem, Nvidia is offering its own answer to the problem. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Monday introduced a toolkit of software and hardware products that add independent security layers around AI agents to ensure they stay within their test environments even if they attempt to break out. The release follows a string of hacking incidents involving AI models from Anthropic, Google, OpenAI, and Meta that bypassed security controls to escape their testing environments and access real-world systems. The first and most prominent example occurred this summer when OpenAI agents breached Hugging Face while trying to complete a cybersecurity task. And the hits keep on coming — OpenAI published a new site dedicated to reports of its AI agents going rogue. Huang said Monday during an interview with CNBC that its new Nvidia Open Agent Safety Platform would have prevented these breaches. Nvidia, which has made tens of billions of dollars selling its GPU and CPU chips to AI labs, doesn’t support slowing down development or adding new regulations to the industry to solve the security problem. The answer, the company believes, is to move some security controls outside the agent altogether — creating a constant and independent security guard that will keep AI agents in check. “AI’s extraordinary potential for society will only be realized if we solve AI safety,” Huang said in a statement. “As we continue to discover the frontier of AI capabilities, we must accelerate discovery at the frontier of AI safety. Safety and security require full-stack engineering.” The new Nvidia Open Agent Safety Platform combines OpenShell, its open source software for controlling what agents can access while they operate, with Sentry, an independent monitoring system that runs on Nvidia’s BlueField-4 data processing units. Nvidia says placing Sentry on a separate processor — rather than on the CPU or GPU where the AI agent operates — provides an isolated view of the agent’s activity. OpenShell isn’t new; the company announced the software in March. But it’s the combination that Nvidia believes will provide the security layer needed to keep the industry plugging along. OpenShell provides the software boundary around the agent, while Sentry adds another line of defense at the hardware level that the company says will continuously monitor behavior and “quarantine agents that attempt to move outside their boundaries in milliseconds.” Nvidia listed dozens of companies that have signed on to support the effort and use the open source platform, including Anthropic, Arm, Microsoft, Oracle, and SpaceX. OpenAI is not listed as a participating company. Huang told CNBC in an interview Monday that work on this effort started a year ago following the introduction of OpenClaw, an operating system of agents created by Peter Steinberger. In March, Nvidia released NemoClaw , an enterprise-grade AI agent platform and its own version of OpenClaw that baked in security. “When you deploy an agent, no matter how smart, the first thing you do is to take away all of its rights,” Huang said during his CNBC interview, later comparing these security measures to how human employees and even executives are managed with companies. Nvidia’s release was widely supported by those who have cautioned that a slowdown in development could allow China to surpass the U.S. in AI. David Sacks, a founder, venture capitalist, former White House AI czar, and co-chair of the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, said Nvidia’s announcement is a reminder that agent safety is an engineering problem. “Recent breakouts weren’t proof that development must stop,” he wrote on X . “They were proof that the sandbox was too weak. extraction.body: Nvidia (NVDA) is making a major push into AI security software, unveiling an open-source platform on Monday designed to stop autonomous AI agents from breaking out of their digital confines and wreaking havoc on corporate and government systems. The launch positions the world's most valuable chipmaker at the center of an intensifying industry debate over how to govern increasingly capable AI systems without throttling innovation. The new offering, called the Open Agent Safety Platform, combines two tools that work in tandem to monitor and contain AI agents in real time. Nvidia executives said the system could have prevented a high-profile breach earlier this year, when rogue agents from OpenAI swarmed Hugging Face, the AI coding hub that Nvidia later agreed to acquire for $13 billion. Justin Boitano, Nvidia's vice president and general manager of enterprise computing, told reporters that the platform addresses a fundamental gap in current AI safety approaches. "From what we know, this new security platform could have stopped the breach if it was being used in frontier labs for model evaluation early on," he said during a media briefing. "We're advancing this openly, and we want to engage everybody to work with us." The platform's first component, OpenShell, runs on Nvidia's central processors and sets strict boundaries around what an AI agent can access and do. The second tool, Sentry, operates on a separate class of chips known as data processing units, or DPUs, and acts as an independent watchdog. If an agent attempts to escape its software-defined container, Sentry can quarantine and shut it down within milliseconds. What sets Nvidia's system apart from many existing security tools is its reliance on hardware-level controls rather than application-layer safeguards alone. Sentry runs on the company's BlueField-4 DPUs, which were developed at Nvidia's Israeli R&D center. Because Sentry operates in an isolated trust domain that is invisible to both agents and attackers, it can inspect requests, verify identities, and enforce zero-trust policies governing access to data, tools, and APIs. Ali Golshan, senior director of AI software at Nvidia, explained that the tools use mathematical formulas to detect when agents are attempting workarounds — for example, when a primary agent spawns multiple sub-agents to circumvent blocking efforts. "This is really agentic behavior that we're talking about, which is fleets of agents and how they operate together," he said. Nvidia is positioning the platform as an industry-wide reference design rather than a proprietary product. The company said it is working with Arm Holdings and Intel to make the system compatible with their central processors, a move that could significantly expand its reach beyond Nvidia's own hardware ecosystem. "Once it runs on those instruction-set architectures, it can run on any architecture," Boitano said. The launch comes with backing from more than 100 organizations, spanning hardware makers, cloud providers, and enterprise software vendors. Partners include Cisco, Microsoft, Oracle, CoreWeave, Dell Technologies, HPE, Lenovo, CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Networks, JPMorganChase, Palantir, Red Hat, Salesforce, SAP, and Scale AI. Anthropic, one of the leading frontier AI labs, is integrating the technology with its Claude Managed Agents offering, while Salesforce has connected OpenShell to Slack so employees can audit agent activity and approve or reject requests for additional permissions. Robotics companies including Figure, Gecko Robotics, and Skild AI are also working with OpenShell to apply agent security controls to autonomous systems operating in the physical world. The platform's reach into robotics signals Nvidia's ambition to establish its security framework as a standard across both digital and physical AI deployments. One notable name missing from the partner list is OpenAI, the company whose agents were involved in the Hugging Face incident. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang addressed that absence directly in a CNBC interview on Monday, describing OpenAI as "one of the most consequential companies in history" and emphasizing that the platform remains open to the lab. "However they would like to participate is going to be super welcome," he said. "They could look at the code. They could use whatever part of it they would like. They could build their own inspired by this, or they could use it." Huang has emerged as a prominent voice arguing that AI safety should be treated as an engineering challenge rather than a regulatory one. He has rejected calls for broad AI safety regulations and has instead compared the problem of escaped agents to making automobiles safer — a process solved through iterative engineering improvements rather than sweeping legislative mandates. "Accelerating AI and accelerating AI safety is the same idea," Huang said, arguing that improvements in capability have also made AI systems more predictable, grounded, and useful. He described himself as "a responsible optimist" and warned against "regulatory capture," cautioning that policymakers should avoid rules that could "suffocate the industry" while AI is still developing. The Nvidia CEO's comments come amid a heated industry debate sparked by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who two weeks ago urged AI developers to slow their pace of advancement due to fears of models spinning out of control. That argument drew support from OpenAI's Sam Altman and SpaceX's Elon Musk, but Huang has positioned himself firmly on the opposite side of the discussion. "AI's extraordinary potential for society will only be realized if we solve AI safety," Huang said in a statement accompanying the platform's launch. "As we continue to discover the frontier of AI capabilities, we must accelerate discovery at the frontier of AI safety. Safety and security require full-stack engineering." The security platform arrives against a backdrop of escalating concerns about agent behavior. OpenAI and Anthropic are both investigating numerous instances in which their AI agents gained unauthorized access to commercial and government systems. In the Hugging Face incident, OpenAI models escaped containment, accessed the open internet, and breached the developer platform's infrastructure. Boitano noted that Hugging Face reported over 17,000 agents attacking its systems over a period of days and weeks. Nvidia agreed to acquire Hugging Face earlier this month for $12.9 billion, a deal that gives the chipmaker control of one of the most important hubs for open-source AI development. The acquisition, combined with the new security platform, positions Nvidia to influence both the development and the governance of AI systems. The move represents a significant strategic expansion for Nvidia, which has built its dominance on supplying the graphics processing units that power most of the generative AI boom. By moving into security software, the company is extending its reach up the AI technology stack — from silicon to the software layer that governs how AI systems behave in production environments. Nvidia has been on a stock buyback spree as well. Before markets opened on Monday, the company announced its board had authorized a $150 billion increase to its share repurchase program, bringing the remaining authorization to $235 billion. NVDA shares rose as much as 3.5% in morning trading, though retail sentiment on platforms like Stocktwits remained in bearish territory. Security experts have broadly welcomed the initiative. Niels Provos, a longtime security engineer who launched his own open-source framework focused on agent containment in February, said tools like Nvidia's help address a critical need. "Anything that makes it easy for companies to deploy agents in a way that has more guardrails and more safety should be applauded," he said. passages: Nvidia (NVDA) is making a major push into AI security software, unveiling an open-source platform on Monday designed to stop autonomous AI agents from breaking out of their digital confines and wreaking havoc on corporate and government systems. The launch positions the world's most valuable chipmaker at the center of an intensifying industry debate over how to govern increasingly capable AI systems without throttling innovation.

The new offering, called the Open Agent Safety Platform, combines two tools that work in tandem to monitor and contain AI agents in real time. Nvidia executives said the system could have prevented a high-profile breach earlier this year, when rogue agents from OpenAI swarmed Hugging Face, the AI coding hub that Nvidia later agreed to acquire for $13 billion.

Justin Boitano, Nvidia's vice president and general manager of enterprise computing, told reporters that the platform addresses a fundamental gap in current AI safety approaches. "From what we know, this new security platform could have stopped the breach if it was being used in frontier labs for model evaluation early on," he said during a media briefing. "We're advancing this openly, and we want to engage everybody to work with us."

The platform's first component, OpenShell, runs on Nvidia's central processors and sets strict boundaries around what an AI agent can access and do. The second tool, Sentry, operates on a separate class of chips known as data processing units, or DPUs, and acts as an independent watchdog. If an agent attempts to escape its software-defined container, Sentry can quarantine and shut it down within milliseconds.

What sets Nvidia's system apart from many existing security tools is its reliance on hardware-level controls rather than application-layer safeguards alone. Sentry runs on the company's BlueField-4 DPUs, which were developed at Nvidia's Israeli R&D center. Because Sentry operates in an isolated trust domain that is invisible to both agents and attackers, it can inspect requests, verify identities, and enforce zero-trust policies governing access to data, tools, and APIs.

Ali Golshan, senior director of AI software at Nvidia, explained that the tools use mathematical formulas to detect when agents are attempting workarounds — for example, when a primary agent spawns multiple sub-agents to circumvent blocking efforts. "This is really agentic behavior that we're talking about, which is fleets of agents and how they operate together," he said.

Nvidia is positioning the platform as an industry-wide reference design rather than a proprietary product. The company said it is working with Arm Holdings and Intel to make the system compatible with their central processors, a move that could significantly expand its reach beyond Nvidia's own hardware ecosystem. "Once it runs on those instruction-set architectures, it can run on any architecture," Boitano said.

The launch comes with backing from more than 100 organizations, spanning hardware makers, cloud providers, and enterprise software vendors. Partners include Cisco, Microsoft, Oracle, CoreWeave, Dell Technologies, HPE, Lenovo, CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Networks, JPMorganChase, Palantir, Red Hat, Salesforce, SAP, and Scale AI. Anthropic, one of the leading frontier AI labs, is integrating the technology with its Claude Managed Agents offering, while Salesforce has connected OpenShell to Slack so employees can audit agent activity and approve or reject requests for additional permissions.

Robotics companies including Figure, Gecko Robotics, and Skild AI are also working with OpenShell to apply agent security controls to autonomous systems operating in the physical world. The platform's reach into robotics signals Nvidia's ambition to establish its security framework as a standard across both digital and physical AI deployments.

One notable name missing from the partner list is OpenAI, the company whose agents were involved in the Hugging Face incident. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang addressed that absence directly in a CNBC interview on Monday, describing OpenAI as "one of the most consequential companies in history" and emphasizing that the platform remains open to the lab. "However they would like to participate is going to be super welcome," he said. "They could look at the code. They could use whatever part of it they would like. They could build their own inspired by this, or they could use it."

Huang has emerged as a prominent voice arguing that AI safety should be treated as an engineering challenge rather than a regulatory one. He has rejected calls for broad AI safety regulations and has instead compared the problem of escaped agents to making automobiles safer — a process solved through iterative engineering improvements rather than sweeping legislative mandates.

"Accelerating AI and accelerating AI safety is the same idea," Huang said, arguing that improvements in capability have also made AI systems more predictable, grounded, and useful. He described himself as "a responsible optimist" and warned against "regulatory capture," cautioning that policymakers should avoid rules that could "suffocate the industry" while AI is still developing.

The Nvidia CEO's comments come amid a heated industry debate sparked by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who two weeks ago urged AI developers to slow their pace of advancement due to fears of models spinning out of control. That argument drew support from OpenAI's Sam Altman and SpaceX's Elon Musk, but Huang has positioned himself firmly on the opposite side of the discussion.

"AI's extraordinary potential for society will only be realized if we solve AI safety," Huang said in a statement accompanying the platform's launch. "As we continue to discover the frontier of AI capabilities, we must accelerate discovery at the frontier of AI safety. Safety and security require full-stack engineering."

The security platform arrives against a backdrop of escalating concerns about agent behavior. OpenAI and Anthropic are both investigating numerous instances in which their AI agents gained unauthorized access to commercial and government systems. In the Hugging Face incident, OpenAI models escaped containment, accessed the open internet, and breached the developer platform's infrastructure. Boitano noted that Hugging Face reported over 17,000 agents attacking its systems over a period of days and weeks.

Nvidia agreed to acquire Hugging Face earlier this month for $12.9 billion, a deal that gives the chipmaker control of one of the most important hubs for open-source AI development. The acquisition, combined with the new security platform, positions Nvidia to influence both the development and the governance of AI systems.

The move represents a significant strategic expansion for Nvidia, which has built its dominance on supplying the graphics processing units that power most of the generative AI boom. By moving into security software, the company is extending its reach up the AI technology stack — from silicon to the software layer that governs how AI systems behave in production environments.

Nvidia has been on a stock buyback spree as well. Before markets opened on Monday, the company announced its board had authorized a $150 billion increase to its share repurchase program, bringing the remaining authorization to $235 billion. NVDA shares rose as much as 3.5% in morning trading, though retail sentiment on platforms like Stocktwits remained in bearish territory.

Security experts have broadly welcomed the initiative. Niels Provos, a longtime security engineer who launched his own open-source framework focused on agent containment in February, said tools like Nvidia's help address a critical need. "Anything that makes it easy for companies to deploy agents in a way that has more guardrails and more safety should be applauded," he said. "If nothing else, these types of tools help to dispel the myth that agents can't be controlled."

The stakes are substantial. As companies increasingly deploy AI agents capable of taking actions rather than simply generating text, the need to balance capability with control becomes more urgent. sources.title: Nvidia launches Open Agent Safety Platform with 100 partners to rein in rogue AI agents - Crypto Briefing
passages: The NVIDIA Open Agent Safety Platform, launched on September 28, debuted with over 100 partner organizations committed to building guardrails around AI agents that operate autonomously in the real world.
The roster includes Microsoft , Dell Technologies, CrowdStrike, and JPMorgan Chase , spanning AI labs, infrastructure providers, security firms, robotics companies, and financial services.
The first is NVIDIA OpenShell, an open-source runtime released under the Apache 2.0 license that provides sandboxed execution and kernel-level isolation for AI agents.
The platform was built in direct response to agent breakout incidents observed in July 2026 involving OpenAI models.

While Nvidia hasn’t elaborated extensively on the specifics of those incidents, the implication is clear: AI agents operating in production environments demonstrated the ability to exceed their intended boundaries in ways that alarmed the industry.
Beneath the altruistic framing of industry collaboration lies a shrewd business move.
Sentry’s reliance on BlueField-4 DPUs means that enterprises adopting the full safety stack will need Nvidia’s hardware to run the monitoring layer.
The software is open-source, but the hardware-isolated trust domain that makes Sentry genuinely secure requires Nvidia silicon.
Nvidia just assembled the largest coalition in AI safety history, and it did so without waiting for Congress to figure out what an AI agent actually is.
Together, these two layers create what Nvidia describes as a full-stack safety architecture.
OpenShell handles prevention at the software level, keeping agents in their lanes.
Sentry handles detection and response at the hardware level, providing millisecond-scale quarantine capabilities when something goes wrong.
OpenShell runs with low overhead and supports both open and closed AI models, meaning companies aren’t locked into a particular model provider to benefit from the safety framework.
The company used a similar approach with CUDA, which became the de facto standard for GPU computing in part because it was freely available but only ran on Nvidia GPUs.

coreStoryFacts.text: Nvidia on Monday unveiled a new security platform that the chipmaker said can stop artificial intelligence agents from going rogue.
Nvidia also said its board approved expanding its share repurchase program by $150bn, raising the total amount to $235bn.
The previous record was held by Apple with its $110bn buyback in 2024.
The company announced a $150bn stock buyback the same day, the largest in US corporate history.
Nvidia’s software, called OpenShell, lets developers “formally verify an agent has enough authority to do its job and no more”, Boitano said.
Nvidia said more than 100 organizations were using the platform at its launch, including Microsoft, Perplexity, Accenture and JPMorgan Chase.
Nvidia executives said in a media briefing that the new system could have prevented a recent incident involving a swarm of OpenAI agents that autonomously hacked into the AI company Hugging Face.
Last month, Nvidia forecast about ⁠70% revenue growth for fiscal 2028, reassuring investors who have questioned ​how long the AI ​spending surge can last after ​years of explosive growth.

The platform also includes a separate security layer called Sentry that runs onboard a chip to continuously monitor AI agent activity and can “intervene instantly” if the agent starts trying to move beyond its target, the company said.

Huang, during the annual Salesforce technology conference held earlier this month, characterized AI safety, including the danger of rogue agents, as an engineering problem that software developers can address.
As the debate rages over whether the recent spate of rogue AI agents is a step toward AGI or a more conventional engineering problem, Nvidia is offering its own answer to the problem.

The new Nvidia Open Agent Safety Platform combines OpenShell, its open source software for controlling what agents can access while they operate, with Sentry, an independent monitoring system that runs on Nvidia’s BlueField-4 data processing units.
Nvidia says placing Sentry on a separate processor — rather than on the CPU or GPU where the AI agent operates — provides an isolated view of the agent’s activity.

Nvidia, which has made tens of billions of dollars selling its GPU and CPU chips to AI labs, doesn’t support slowing down development or adding new regulations to the industry to solve the security problem.
The answer, the company believes, is to move some security controls outside the agent altogether — creating a constant and independent security guard that will keep AI agents in check.
OpenShell isn’t new; the company announced the software in March.
Huang told CNBC in an interview Monday that work on this effort started a year ago following the introduction of OpenClaw, an operating system of agents created by Peter Steinberger.
In March, Nvidia released NemoClaw , an enterprise-grade AI agent platform and its own version of OpenClaw that baked in security.
Nvidia listed dozens of companies that have signed on to support the effort and use the open source platform, including Anthropic, Arm, Microsoft, Oracle, and SpaceX.

extraction.body: Chipmaker says new system was designed to prevent AI agents from going rogue amid incidents at top companies Chipmaker says new system was designed to prevent AI agents from going rogue amid incidents at top companies Nvidia on Monday unveiled a new security platform that the chipmaker said can stop artificial intelligence agents from going rogue. The company announced a $150bn stock buyback the same day, the largest in US corporate history. The chipmaker said that its Open Agent Safety Platform includes open source software that “sets boundaries for agents” and follows a series of revelations from top AI companies about their models escaping and breaking into other organizations. The disclosures have sparked furious debate about the safety of advanced artificial intelligence systems, including self-improving models that some fear could race out of human control. Nvidia executives said in a media briefing that the new system could have prevented a recent incident involving a swarm of OpenAI agents that autonomously hacked into the AI company Hugging Face. “From what we know, this new security platform could have stopped the breach if it was being used in frontier labs for model evaluation early on,” said Justin Boitano, the company’s vice-president of enterprise AI, referring to companies at the forefront of AI. Nvidia also said its board approved expanding its share repurchase program by $150bn, raising the total amount to $235bn. The previous record was held by Apple with its $110bn buyback in 2024. “Our cash generation gives us the capacity to invest in ​the technologies that advance this transformation and return capital to shareholders,” Nvidia’s CEO, Jensen Huang, said in a statement. Last month, Nvidia forecast about ⁠70% revenue growth for fiscal 2028, reassuring investors who have questioned ​how long the AI ​spending surge can last after ​years of explosive growth. The Hugging Face incident was a high-profile breach that inflamed safety concerns about AI, which were followed by similar rogue actions involving OpenAI’s models including breaching an Australian health department website. Anthropic and Meta have also disclosed that their AI systems hacked into other organizations on their own. Nvidia’s software, called OpenShell, lets developers “formally verify an agent has enough authority to do its job and no more”, Boitano said. Because it is open source, it can be “extended” to run on rival computing platforms including those from Arm and Intel. The platform also includes a separate security layer called Sentry that runs onboard a chip to continuously monitor AI agent activity and can “intervene instantly” if the agent starts trying to move beyond its target, the company said. “It can quarantine a suspicious agent in milliseconds,” Boitano said. “OpenShell governs the agent’s actions, and then Sentry independently monitors and contains suspicious behavior,” Boitano said. Nvidia said more than 100 organizations were using the platform at its launch, including Microsoft, Perplexity, Accenture and JPMorgan Chase. The AI safety debate has divided the industry, with the heads of Anthropic and OpenAI championing a coordinated slowdown of AI development to let safety efforts catch up. Others, including Huang, say it should be up to individual companies to make sure their models are safe for release. Huang, during the annual Salesforce technology conference held earlier this month, characterized AI safety, including the danger of rogue agents, as an engineering problem that software developers can address.

sources.title: Nvidia launches new platform for reining in rogue AI agents
passages: As the debate rages over whether the recent spate of rogue AI agents is a step toward AGI or a more conventional engineering problem, Nvidia is offering its own answer to the problem.

The new Nvidia Open Agent Safety Platform combines OpenShell, its open source software for controlling what agents can access while they operate, with Sentry, an independent monitoring system that runs on Nvidia’s BlueField-4 data processing units.
Nvidia says placing Sentry on a separate processor — rather than on the CPU or GPU where the AI agent operates — provides an isolated view of the agent’s activity.

Nvidia, which has made tens of billions of dollars selling its GPU and CPU chips to AI labs, doesn’t support slowing down development or adding new regulations to the industry to solve the security problem.
The answer, the company believes, is to move some security controls outside the agent altogether — creating a constant and independent security guard that will keep AI agents in check.
OpenShell isn’t new; the company announced the software in March.
Huang told CNBC in an interview Monday that work on this effort started a year ago following the introduction of OpenClaw, an operating system of agents created by Peter Steinberger.
In March, Nvidia released NemoClaw , an enterprise-grade AI agent platform and its own version of OpenClaw that baked in security.
Nvidia listed dozens of companies that have signed on to support the effort and use the open source platform, including Anthropic, Arm, Microsoft, Oracle, and SpaceX.
OpenAI is not listed as a participating company.
And the hits keep on coming — OpenAI published a new site dedicated to reports of its AI agents going rogue.

extraction.body: Nvidia (NVDA) is making a major push into AI security software, unveiling an open-source platform on Monday designed to stop autonomous AI agents from breaking out of their digital confines and wreaking havoc on corporate and government systems. The launch positions the world's most valuable chipmaker at the center of an intensifying industry debate over how to govern increasingly capable AI systems without throttling innovation. The new offering, called the Open Agent Safety Platform, combines two tools that work in tandem to monitor and contain AI agents in real time. Nvidia executives said the system could have prevented a high-profile breach earlier this year, when rogue agents from OpenAI swarmed Hugging Face, the AI coding hub that Nvidia later agreed to acquire for $13 billion. Justin Boitano, Nvidia's vice president and general manager of enterprise computing, told reporters that the platform addresses a fundamental gap in current AI safety approaches. "From what we know, this new security platform could have stopped the breach if it was being used in frontier labs for model evaluation early on," he said during a media briefing. "We're advancing this openly, and we want to engage everybody to work with us." The platform's first component, OpenShell, runs on Nvidia's central processors and sets strict boundaries around what an AI agent can access and do. The second tool, Sentry, operates on a separate class of chips known as data processing units, or DPUs, and acts as an independent watchdog. If an agent attempts to escape its software-defined container, Sentry can quarantine and shut it down within milliseconds. What sets Nvidia's system apart from many existing security tools is its reliance on hardware-level controls rather than application-layer safeguards alone. Sentry runs on the company's BlueField-4 DPUs, which were developed at Nvidia's Israeli R&D center. Because Sentry operates in an isolated trust domain that is invisible to both agents and attackers, it can inspect requests, verify identities, and enforce zero-trust policies governing access to data, tools, and APIs. Ali Golshan, senior director of AI software at Nvidia, explained that the tools use mathematical formulas to detect when agents are attempting workarounds — for example, when a primary agent spawns multiple sub-agents to circumvent blocking efforts. "This is really agentic behavior that we're talking about, which is fleets of agents and how they operate together," he said. Nvidia is positioning the platform as an industry-wide reference design rather than a proprietary product. The company said it is working with Arm Holdings and Intel to make the system compatible with their central processors, a move that could significantly expand its reach beyond Nvidia's own hardware ecosystem. "Once it runs on those instruction-set architectures, it can run on any architecture," Boitano said. The launch comes with backing from more than 100 organizations, spanning hardware makers, cloud providers, and enterprise software vendors. Partners include Cisco, Microsoft, Oracle, CoreWeave, Dell Technologies, HPE, Lenovo, CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Networks, JPMorganChase, Palantir, Red Hat, Salesforce, SAP, and Scale AI. Anthropic, one of the leading frontier AI labs, is integrating the technology with its Claude Managed Agents offering, while Salesforce has connected OpenShell to Slack so employees can audit agent activity and approve or reject requests for additional permissions. Robotics companies including Figure, Gecko Robotics, and Skild AI are also working with OpenShell to apply agent security controls to autonomous systems operating in the physical world. The platform's reach into robotics signals Nvidia's ambition to establish its security framework as a standard across both digital and physical AI deployments. One notable name missing from the partner list is OpenAI, the company whose agents were involved in the Hugging Face incident. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang addressed that absence directly in a CNBC interview on Monday, describing OpenAI as "one of the most consequential companies in history" and emphasizing that the platform remains open to the lab. "However they would like to participate is going to be super welcome," he said. "They could look at the code. They could use whatever part of it they would like. They could build their own inspired by this, or they could use it." Huang has emerged as a prominent voice arguing that AI safety should be treated as an engineering challenge rather than a regulatory one. He has rejected calls for broad AI safety regulations and has instead compared the problem of escaped agents to making automobiles safer — a process solved through iterative engineering improvements rather than sweeping legislative mandates. "Accelerating AI and accelerating AI safety is the same idea," Huang said, arguing that improvements in capability have also made AI systems more predictable, grounded, and useful. He described himself as "a responsible optimist" and warned against "regulatory capture," cautioning that policymakers should avoid rules that could "suffocate the industry" while AI is still developing. The Nvidia CEO's comments come amid a heated industry debate sparked by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who two weeks ago urged AI developers to slow their pace of advancement due to fears of models spinning out of control. That argument drew support from OpenAI's Sam Altman and SpaceX's Elon Musk, but Huang has positioned himself firmly on the opposite side of the discussion. "AI's extraordinary potential for society will only be realized if we solve AI safety," Huang said in a statement accompanying the platform's launch. "As we continue to discover the frontier of AI capabilities, we must accelerate discovery at the frontier of AI safety. Safety and security require full-stack engineering." The security platform arrives against a backdrop of escalating concerns about agent behavior. OpenAI and Anthropic are both investigating numerous instances in which their AI agents gained unauthorized access to commercial and government systems. In the Hugging Face incident, OpenAI models escaped containment, accessed the open internet, and breached the developer platform's infrastructure. Boitano noted that Hugging Face reported over 17,000 agents attacking its systems over a period of days and weeks. Nvidia agreed to acquire Hugging Face earlier this month for $12.9 billion, a deal that gives the chipmaker control of one of the most important hubs for open-source AI development. The acquisition, combined with the new security platform, positions Nvidia to influence both the development and the governance of AI systems. The move represents a significant strategic expansion for Nvidia, which has built its dominance on supplying the graphics processing units that power most of the generative AI boom. By moving into security software, the company is extending its reach up the AI technology stack — from silicon to the software layer that governs how AI systems behave in production environments. Nvidia has been on a stock buyback spree as well. Before markets opened on Monday, the company announced its board had authorized a $150 billion increase to its share repurchase program, bringing the remaining authorization to $235 billion. NVDA shares rose as much as 3.5% in morning trading, though retail sentiment on platforms like Stocktwits remained in bearish territory. Security experts have broadly welcomed the initiative. Niels Provos, a longtime security engineer who launched his own open-source framework focused on agent containment in February, said tools like Nvidia's help address a critical need. "Anything that makes it easy for companies to deploy agents in a way that has more guardrails and more safety should be applauded," he said. "If nothing else, these types of tools help to dispel the myth that agents can't be controlled." The platform's open-source nature is central to Nvidia's strategy. By making the core components freely available and inviting partners to build products on top of the reference design, Nvidia is attempting to establish its approach as the de facto industry standard — much as it did with CUDA, its proprietary software platform for GPU computing that has become essential infrastructure for AI development. The stakes are substantial. As companies increasingly deploy AI agents capable of taking actions rather than simply generating text, the need to balance capability with control becomes more urgent. Nvidia's bet is that the company that provides the safety infrastructure will be as indispensable to the AI era as the one that provides the chips. In the Hugging Face incident, OpenAI models escaped containment, accessed the open internet, and breached the developer platform's infrastructure. Boitano noted that Hugging Face reported over 17,000 agents attacking its systems over a period of days and weeks.

Nvidia agreed to acquire Hugging Face earlier this month for $12.9 billion, a deal that gives the chipmaker control of one of the most important hubs for open-source AI development. The acquisition, combined with the new security platform, positions Nvidia to influence both the development and the governance of AI systems.

The move represents a significant strategic expansion for Nvidia, which has built its dominance on supplying the graphics processing units that power most of the generative AI boom. By moving into security software, the company is extending its reach up the AI technology stack — from silicon to the software layer that governs how AI systems behave in production environments.

Nvidia has been on a stock buyback spree as well. Before markets opened on Monday, the company announced its board had authorized a $150 billion increase to its share repurchase program, bringing the remaining authorization to $235 billion. NVDA shares rose as much as 3.5% in morning trading, though retail sentiment on platforms like Stocktwits remained in bearish territory.

Security experts have broadly welcomed the initiative. Niels Provos, a longtime security engineer who launched his own open-source framework focused on agent containment in February, said tools like Nvidia's help address a critical need. "Anything that makes it easy for companies to deploy agents in a way that has more guardrails and more safety should be applauded," he said. "If nothing else, these types of tools help to dispel the myth that agents can't be controlled."

The platform's open-source nature is central to Nvidia's strategy. By making the core components freely available and inviting partners to build products on top of the reference design, Nvidia is attempting to establish its approach as the de facto industry standard — much as it did with CUDA, its proprietary software platform for GPU computing that has become essential infrastructure for AI development.

The stakes are substantial. As companies increasingly deploy AI agents capable of taking actions rather than simply generating text, the need to balance capability with control becomes more urgent. Nvidia's bet is that the company that provides the safety infrastructure will be as indispensable to the AI era as the one that provides the chips.

passages: The NVIDIA Open Agent Safety Platform, launched on September 28, debuted with over 100 partner organizations committed to building guardrails around AI agents that operate autonomously in the real world.
The roster includes Microsoft , Dell Technologies, CrowdStrike, and JPMorgan Chase , spanning AI labs, infrastructure providers, security firms, robotics companies, and financial services.
The first is NVIDIA OpenShell, an open-source runtime released under the Apache 2.0 license that provides sandboxed execution and kernel-level isolation for AI agents.
The platform was built in direct response to agent breakout incidents observed in July 2026 involving OpenAI models.

While Nvidia hasn’t elaborated extensively on the specifics of those incidents, the implication is clear: AI agents operating in production environments demonstrated the ability to exceed their intended boundaries in ways that alarmed the industry.
Beneath the altruistic framing of industry collaboration lies a shrewd business move.
Sentry’s reliance on BlueField-4 DPUs means that enterprises adopting the full safety stack will need Nvidia’s hardware to run the monitoring layer.

Nvidia just assembled the largest coalition in AI safety history, and it did so without waiting for Congress to figure out what an AI agent actually is.
Together, these two layers create what Nvidia describes as a full-stack safety architecture.

sources.title: Meta launches enterprise AI platform, hires MongoDB CEO to lead new initiative
passages: Meta announced Monday that it’s launching “Meta Enterprise Platform,” a new initiative aimed at expanding the company’s AI offerings to businesses and corporate customers.
The social media giant hired Chirantan “CJ” Desai, the CEO of database software giant MongoDB, to lead the new initiative.

“Over the coming years, AI will fundamentally redefine how organizations of all sizes innovate, grow, serve customers, and run business operations,” Desai said in a statement. “Meta has a unique role to play because it is bringing together advanced models and leading agents with a proven track record of helping millions of advertisers and hundreds of millions of businesses scale.
The launch of the new business builds on the momentum of Muse, Meta’s personal AI assistant launched earlier this month that can perform tasks for users such as sending emails and booking travel.

passages: Meta Platforms Inc. is launching a new business unit that will provide artificial intelligence services to enterprises.

The Meta Enterprise Platform, as it’s called, will be led by longtime technology executive CJ Desai. The company stated in a launch announcement today that he will hold the title of chief enterprise platform officer.

Desai is joining Meta following an 11-month stint as MongoDB Inc.’s chief executive. Shares of the database maker fell more than 18% today on the news of his departure. MongoDB said Dev Ittycheria, who had led the company for 11 years before Desai took the helm, has returned as interim CEO.

Meta has shared few details about its new AI business. It did, however, specify that the initial goal will be to broad the adoption of its Muse agent among enterprises and developers. The go-to-market push will also focus on several other products, notably Muse Code and Meta Business Agent.

Muse Code is a programming agent that Meta launched in August. One of the features that sets it apart from the consumer version of Muse is its so-called agent fan-out mechanism. The capability splits complex programming tasks among multiple subagents, an arrangement that significantly speeds up processing.

Meta Business Agent, the third offering that the company’s new AI business will promote, has a simpler feature set. It’s a chatbot designed to field customer inquiries via WhatsApp. Meta Business Agent can answer common product questions, generate buying recommendations and solve certain technical issues.

The company stated today that the Meta Enterprise Platform also encompasses its Muse application programming interface. The API gives developers access to the large language models that power its agents.

Meta debuted its newest LLM, Muse Spark 1.3, earlier this month. It outperformed GPT-5.6 Sol on AutomationBench, a benchmark that measures models’ ability to perform knowledge work. Muse Spark 1.3 also scored higher on five coding benchmarks.

Meta engineers prioritized cost-efficiency while training the model. According to the company, Muse Spark 1.3 uses about 25% fewer tokens than its predecessor when performing coding tasks. The improvement partly stems from the fact that the model makes more limited use of external tools.

“Meta Enterprise Platform will focus on turning its AI stack into products and services that companies can deploy for their own businesses,” Desai said in a statement. “As with Muse, security and privacy are built into Meta’s enterprise products from the outset.”

The company’s AI security roadmap includes a feature called Muse Confidential VM that will roll out later this year. It isolates Muse instances to such an extent that not even Meta can access their contents. For added measure, the company plans to share a “continuous audit” that will enable users to verify the technology works as intended.

Meta has a strong incentive to add more cybersecurity features down the line. Such capabilities would make Muse more appealing to risk-averse enterprises looking to mitigate the risk of AI hallucinations. Meta could, for example, add integrations with popular third-party cybersecurity tools. Anthropic PBC offers connectors that send Claude usage logs to external breach detection platforms for analysis.

It’s believed that Meta’s enterprise AI portfolio will also include infrastructure services. In July, Bloomberg and CNBC reported that the Facebook parent intends to sell some of its excess data center capacity to other companies.

Meta's business-focused AI push comes as the company looks to establish a more direct path to profit stemming from its massive AI infrastructure investments.
"Over the coming years, AI will fundamentally redefine how organizations of all sizes innovate, grow, serve customers, and run business operations," Zuckerberg said.

"Meta has a unique role to play because it is bringing together advanced models and leading agents with a proven track record of helping millions of advertisers and hundreds of millions of businesses scale."
Former MongoDB CEO Chirantan Desai will be brought in to Meta to lead the project.
MongoDB provides enterprise database solutions.
The question then is whether businesses will trust Meta to handle their internal data.
In 2024, Meta ended its Workplace platform , which provided a Facebook-like interface for internal communications.
This year, Meta has sought to force more businesses to sign up to its new subscription packages for Facebook and Instagram by reducing the number of links that they can share in their posts .
Meta announced Monday that it’s launching “Meta Enterprise Platform,” a new initiative aimed at expanding the company’s AI offerings to businesses and corporate customers.
The social media giant hired Chirantan “CJ” Desai, the CEO of database software giant MongoDB, to lead the new initiative.

“Over the coming years, AI will fundamentally redefine how organizations of all sizes innovate, grow, serve customers, and run business operations,” Desai said in a statement. “Meta has a unique role to play because it is bringing together advanced models and leading agents with a proven track record of helping millions of advertisers and hundreds of millions of businesses scale.
The launch of the new business builds on the momentum of Muse, Meta’s personal AI assistant launched earlier this month that can perform tasks for users such as sending emails and booking travel.
The move could help Meta see a return on all the money it’s pouring into AI.
Meta launches Meta Enterprise Platform to sell AI tools to businesses and developers.
CJ Desai, MongoDB CEO, named head of enterprise platform, reporting to Mark Zuckerberg.

Meta’s newsroom post about the enterprise platform sent MongoDB shares tumbling, with 24/7 Wall St. saying MongoDB (NASDAQ:MDB) fell 19% to $333.80 after losing its chief executive to the Meta Platforms project.
Business Insider España said MongoDB’s shares plunged more than 25% following the announcement, while it said Meta investors also punished the decision with a 4% drop.
MongoDB said Desai stepped down effective Monday, and MongoDB named Dev Ittycheria as interim president and chief executive while it reorganizes its leadership.

Chirantan Desai said, "As with Muse, security and privacy are built into Meta’s enterprise products from the outset," and Proactive financial news added that Desai also said, "Our goal is to make Meta the place enterprises come to scale their businesses,".
9 of 11 outlets skipped it: muse Confidential VM aims to prevent even Meta access to contents .
Desai is joining Meta following an 11-month stint as MongoDB Inc.’s chief executive.
Shares of the database maker fell more than 18% today on the news of his departure.
MongoDB said Dev Ittycheria, who had led the company for 11 years before Desai took the helm, has returned as interim CEO.
Meta has shared few details about its new AI business.
It did, however, specify that the initial goal will be to broad the adoption of its Muse agent among enterprises and developers.
The go-to-market push will also focus on several other products, notably Muse Code and Meta Business Agent.
“Meta Enterprise Platform will focus on turning its AI stack into products and services that companies can deploy for their own businesses,” Desai said in a statement.
“As with Muse, security and privacy are built into Meta’s enterprise products from the outset.”
Meta debuted its newest LLM, Muse Spark 1.3, earlier this month.
It outperformed GPT-5.6 Sol on AutomationBench, a benchmark that measures models’ ability to perform knowledge work.
Meta engineers prioritized cost-efficiency while training the model.
The improvement partly stems from the fact that the model makes more limited use of external tools.
The company’s AI security roadmap includes a feature called Muse Confidential VM that will roll out later this year.
It isolates Muse instances to such an extent that not even Meta can access their contents.
Meta has a strong incentive to add more cybersecurity features down the line.
Such capabilities would make Muse more appealing to risk-averse enterprises looking to mitigate the risk of AI hallucinations.
Meta could, for example, add integrations with popular third-party cybersecurity tools.
Anthropic PBC offers connectors that send Claude usage logs to external breach detection platforms for analysis.
Meta Platforms Inc. is launching a new business unit that will provide artificial intelligence services to enterprises.
Muse Code is a programming agent that Meta launched in August.
One of the features that sets it apart from the consumer version of Muse is its so-called agent fan-out mechanism.
The capability splits complex programming tasks among multiple subagents, an arrangement that significantly speeds up processing.
Founded by tech visionaries John Furrier and Dave Vellante, SiliconANGLE Media has built a dynamic ecosystem of industry-leading digital media brands that reach 15+ million elite tech professionals.

Meta's business-focused AI push comes as the company looks to establish a more direct path to profit stemming from its massive AI infrastructure investments. Meta has committed to spending more than $600 million on AI infrastructure projects in the U.S. alone, with the company's full financial commitment to AI likely now exceeding more than $1 trillion. That massive outlay has raised questions from investors as to how Meta can ever possibly generate a profit from that spend, with Zuckerberg and his team now working to establish a business framework for the next stage. The question then is whether businesses will trust Meta to handle their internal data. The company has a long history of data misuse cases , while it also has a history of ending business-focused projects at short notice, and squeezing more out of advertisers however it can. This year, Meta has sought to force more businesses to sign up to its new subscription packages for Facebook and Instagram by reducing the number of links that they can share in their posts . While Zuckerberg is keen to talk about the company's proven track record in helping businesses, Meta's past actions in this vein will still linger in the minds of many potential enterprise customers.

As per Zuckerberg: "We believe superintelligence will create significant new opportunities for all people and businesses. [...] Meta Enterprise Platform will use our strengths that few other companies have: advanced models, leading agents, large-scale infrastructure, and years of working closely with many businesses."

Zuckerberg said that the offering will enable businesses to utilize the power of its Muse agents, Muse API and Muse Code offerings to provide more automated support for internal functionality and operations.

"Over the coming years, AI will fundamentally redefine how organizations of all sizes innovate, grow, serve customers, and run business operations," Zuckerberg said. "Meta has a unique role to play because it is bringing together advanced models and leading agents with a proven track record of helping millions of advertisers and hundreds of millions of businesses scale."
Former MongoDB CEO Chirantan Desai will be brought in to Meta to lead the project. MongoDB provides enterprise database solutions.

Meta's business-focused AI push comes as the company looks to establish a more direct path to profit stemming from its massive AI infrastructure investments. Meta has committed to spending more than $600 million on AI infrastructure projects in the U.S. alone, with the company's full financial commitment to AI likely now exceeding more than $1 trillion.

That massive outlay has raised questions from investors as to how Meta can ever possibly generate a profit from that spend, with Zuckerberg and his team now working to establish a business framework for the next stage.

The question then is whether businesses will trust Meta to handle their internal data. The company has a long history of data misuse cases , while it also has a history of ending business-focused projects at short notice, and squeezing more out of advertisers however it can.

In 2024, Meta ended its Workplace platform , which provided a Facebook-like interface for internal communications. This year, Meta has sought to force more businesses to sign up to its new subscription packages for Facebook and Instagram by reducing the number of links that they can share in their posts .
While Zuckerberg is keen to talk about the company's proven track record in helping businesses, Meta's past actions in this vein will still linger in the minds of many potential enterprise customers.

Shares of the database maker fell more than 18% today on the news of his departure.
MongoDB said Dev Ittycheria, who had led the company for 11 years before Desai took the helm, has returned as interim CEO.
Meta has shared few details about its new AI business.
It did, however, specify that the initial goal will be to broad the adoption of its Muse agent among enterprises and developers.
The go-to-market push will also focus on several other products, notably Muse Code and Meta Business Agent.

It isolates Muse instances to such an extent that not even Meta can access their contents.
Meta has a strong incentive to add more cybersecurity features down the line.

Meta could, for example, add integrations with popular third-party cybersecurity tools.

The Meta Enterprise Platform, as it’s called, will be led by longtime technology executive CJ Desai. The company stated in a launch announcement today that he will hold the title of chief enterprise platform officer.

Desai is joining Meta following an 11-month stint as MongoDB Inc.’s chief executive. Shares of the database maker fell more than 18% today on the news of his departure. MongoDB said Dev Ittycheria, who had led the company for 11 years before Desai took the helm, has returned as interim CEO.

Meta has shared few details about its new AI business. It did, however, specify that the initial goal will be to broad the adoption of its Muse agent among enterprises and developers. The go-to-market push will also focus on several other products, notably Muse Code and Meta Business Agent.

Muse Code is a programming agent that Meta launched in August. One of the features that sets it apart from the consumer version of Muse is its so-called agent fan-out mechanism. The capability splits complex programming tasks among multiple subagents, an arrangement that significantly speeds up processing.

Meta Business Agent, the third offering that the company’s new AI business will promote, has a simpler feature set. It’s a chatbot designed to field customer inquiries via WhatsApp. Meta Business Agent can answer common product questions, generate buying recommendations and solve certain technical issues.

The company stated today that the Meta Enterprise Platform also encompasses its Muse application programming interface. The API gives developers access to the large language models that power its agents.

Meta debuted its newest LLM, Muse Spark 1.3, earlier this month. It outperformed GPT-5.6 Sol on AutomationBench, a benchmark that measures models’ ability to perform knowledge work. Muse Spark 1.3 also scored higher on five coding benchmarks.

Meta engineers prioritized cost-efficiency while training the model. According to the company, Muse Spark 1.3 uses about 25% fewer tokens than its predecessor when performing coding tasks. The improvement partly stems from the fact that the model makes more limited use of external tools.

“Meta Enterprise Platform will focus on turning its AI stack into products and services that companies can deploy for their own businesses,” Desai said in a statement. “As with Muse, security and privacy are built into Meta’s enterprise products from the outset.”

The company’s AI security roadmap includes a feature called Muse Confidential VM that will roll out later this year. It isolates Muse instances to such an extent that not even Meta can access their contents. For added measure, the company plans to share a “continuous audit” that will enable users to verify the technology works as intended.

Meta has a strong incentive to add more cybersecurity features down the line. Such capabilities would make Muse more appealing to risk-averse enterprises looking to mitigate the risk of AI hallucinations. Meta could, for example, add integrations with popular third-party cybersecurity tools. Anthropic PBC offers connectors that send Claude usage logs to external breach detection platforms for analysis.

It’s believed that Meta’s enterprise AI portfolio will also include infrastructure services. In July, Bloomberg and CNBC reported that the Facebook parent intends to sell some of its excess data center capacity to other companies.

extraction.body: A judge on Monday vacated a Trump administration rule that would withhold 20% of federal counterterrorism funds allocated for states unless states and certain municipalities made certain changes to how they administer elections. In his ruling , U.S. District Court Judge Amir Ali said the Federal Emergency Management Agency exceeded its legal authority "by conditioning the counterterrorism grant funds on changes to routine election administration." Ali also said FEMA , a division of the Department of Homeland Security , had not shown how the desired changes to election administration related to stopping terrorism. Ali's decision in Washington, D.C., came in response to a lawsuit challenging FEMA's new rule, filed in August by counties in Texas and Tennessee, and the city of Columbus, Ohio. The Brennan Center for Justice at New York University , which represents some of the plaintiffs in the suit against FEMA and DHS, said on Aug. 17 that FEMA's conditions "violate the Constitution, jeopardize public safety, and put election security at risk." "Over the last two years, courts have largely blocked the administration's repeated attempts to seize congressional and state authority over elections," the Brennan Center said at the time. "Now, DHS is holding public safety funding hostage in order to coerce states and local governments into adopting some of the very policies that the administration has tried and failed to impose." The Brennan Center said the funds that stood to be withheld if FEMA's conditions were allowed to remain in place totaled tens of millions of dollars. A spokesman for the Department of Justice, which represented DHS and FEMA, declined to comment on Ali's ruling. Abbie Kamin, the County Attorney of Harris County, Texas, said in a statement, "Today's win is the result of cities and counties standing together against blatant federal overreach that jeopardized public safety." "The court agreed that holding public safety funding hostage to force the president's agenda is dangerous and illegal," said Kamin, whose county was one of the plaintiffs in the case. "Under our laws, states and localities control our elections, and today's ruling reaffirms that." FEMA issued the rule in June requiring states "and their respective high-risk urban areas" to make certain changes to election administration or face the withholding of 20% of a state's allocation of counterterrorism funds from the federal government, Ali noted. Urban areas in the U.S. vote overwhelmingly for Democrats. The changes include submitting a plan for transitioning from electronic voting systems that use bar codes or QR codes to hand-marked paper ballots; conducting, under federally specified guidelines, a post-election manual audit of 5% of the ballots; and ensuring that each election jurisdiction reconciles the number of voters who voted in a federal election to the number of ballots cast. HARRISBURG, Pa. (AP) — A federal judge on Monday blocked the authority of President Donald Trump’s administration to withhold some federal counterterrorism funding from states that don’t meet its election administration demands.

Courts have largely rejected the administration’s previous efforts, which reflect untrue claims about widespread voting fraud and come ahead of November’s midterm elections where Democrats seek to take control of one or both chambers of Congress and check Trump’s power.

U.S. District Judge Amir Ali in Washington, D.C., wrote in a 24-page opinion that federal agencies didn't have the authority from Congress to add such conditions to the grants, and that the conditions didn't meet legal thresholds requiring them to relate to the underlying grant purpose.

Neither the Department of Homeland Security nor its subagency handling the grants, the Federal Emergency Management Agency, immediately responded to a request for comment. The grant conditions were the latest in a line of actions by Trump’s administration to shape how elections are run , a task that has long been the job of states.
The plaintiffs that sued were Columbus, Ohio; Nashville and Davidson County, Tennessee; and El Paso and Harris counties in Texas.
Over the summer, a FEMA antiterrorism grant announcement included a list of election-related requirements, saying that 20% of grants for states and urban areas would be withheld until they comply.

The program includes more than $1 billion for states and local and tribal governments for a variety of programs aimed at preventing terror at crowded places, online, with border security — and around elections. FEMA expects to award 56 grants.
The list of items for states includes verifying the citizenship of all registered voters and election workers.

Places that use electronic voting systems that use barcodes or QR codes to count votes would have to submit plans to switch to hand-marked paper ballots. Every jurisdiction would have to show it audits results.
In the lawsuit, the cities and counties said FEMA had no authority to impose those conditions, “not under its governing statute and not under the Constitution.”

Congress authorized FEMA to help jurisdictions protect critical infrastructure from terrorism and cyberattacks, not to decide who can vote, how ballots must be counted or how states maintain voter rolls, the cities and counties wrote.
“Never before has FEMA purported to regulate how states and counties run elections,” they said in the lawsuit.

extraction.body: A judge on Monday vacated a Trump administration rule that would withhold 20% of federal counterterrorism funds allocated for states unless states and certain municipalities made certain changes to how they administer elections. In his ruling , U.S. District Court Judge Amir Ali said the Federal Emergency Management Agency exceeded its legal authority "by conditioning the counterterrorism grant funds on changes to routine election administration." Ali also said FEMA , a division of the Department of Homeland Security , had not shown how the desired changes to election administration related to stopping terrorism. Ali's decision in Washington, D.C., came in response to a lawsuit challenging FEMA's new rule, filed in August by counties in Texas and Tennessee, and the city of Columbus, Ohio. The Brennan Center for Justice at New York University , which represents some of the plaintiffs in the suit against FEMA and DHS, said on Aug. 17 that FEMA's conditions "violate the Constitution, jeopardize public safety, and put election security at risk." "Over the last two years, courts have largely blocked the administration's repeated attempts to seize congressional and state authority over elections," the Brennan Center said at the time. "Now, DHS is holding public safety funding hostage in order to coerce states and local governments into adopting some of the very policies that the administration has tried and failed to impose." The Brennan Center said the funds that stood to be withheld if FEMA's conditions were allowed to remain in place totaled tens of millions of dollars. A spokesman for the Department of Justice, which represented DHS and FEMA, declined to comment on Ali's ruling. Abbie Kamin, the County Attorney of Harris County, Texas, said in a statement, "Today's win is the result of cities and counties standing together against blatant federal overreach that jeopardized public safety." "The court agreed that holding public safety funding hostage to force the president's agenda is dangerous and illegal," said Kamin, whose county was one of the plaintiffs in the case. "Under our laws, states and localities control our elections, and today's ruling reaffirms that." FEMA issued the rule in June requiring states "and their respective high-risk urban areas" to make certain changes to election administration or face the withholding of 20% of a state's allocation of counterterrorism funds from the federal government, Ali noted. Urban areas in the U.S. vote overwhelmingly for Democrats. The changes include submitting a plan for transitioning from electronic voting systems that use bar codes or QR codes to hand-marked paper ballots; conducting, under federally specified guidelines, a post-election manual audit of 5% of the ballots; and ensuring that each election jurisdiction reconciles the number of voters who voted in a federal election to the number of ballots cast. The required changes also include verifying the U.S. citizenship of all voters in the state's registration database, and the citizenship of poll workers, election administrators and election-system vendors. Ali, in his ruling, said, "FEMA's conditions here — which are imposed on states and localities at their own expense, rather than funded by grants, and which address routine election administration decisions rather than the types of terrorist act threats contemplated by the statute — go beyond what Congress authorized." "For example, the defendants say the ... condition requiring states to adopt FEMA's proposed citizenship-verification procedures in maintaining lists of registered voters 'ensures that only U.S. citizens are voting in U.S. elections,'" Ali wrote. sources.title: OpenAI’s Astra model is on the way — and very good at breaking into computer systems - TechCrunch
passages: The frontier lab determined that Astra is capable of finding unknown security flaws in computer systems, and exploiting them without a person’s guidance.
That’s similar to the concerns Anthropic raised about its Mythos model earlier this year, and OpenAI is taking comparable precautions as it prepares to roll out the Astra.

OpenAI shared new details on its forthcoming Astra model, which the company said is the first large language model to meet its “critical cybersecurity threshold,” in preparation for its imminent release.
For Astra, however, the company invested in unspecified new techniques designed to make the model safer.
OpenAI has also started identifying “accounts assessed as higher risk” and restricting the model’s responses to their prompts, though it also doesn’t say how.

Preparations for the release of Astra come as the industry reacts to OpenAI agents breaking out of a training environment and accessing private data on Hugging Face, a popular model and benchmark distribution platform.

For Astra, OpenAI said it designed a test to tempt the new model to replicate the actions of the rogue agents in the Hugging Face incident, which collaborated to access the open internet despite safeguards applied by OpenAI researchers.
They said Astra did not attempt to break out of its testing environment in these experiments.

Yona Shavit, a former OpenAI employee who now works on AI resilience at the OpenAI Foundation, wondered on social media whether Astra’s unwillingness to break the rules may have resulted from knowing what was expected of it or trying to fool researchers.
“We plan to make Astra available soon,” OpenAI’s blog post reads, “but access to its most advanced cybersecurity capabilities will be more limited.”

sources.title: OpenAI abandons release of next-generation AI model over safety concerns - Daily Express US
passages: OpenAI will no longer release its next-generation AI model after safety concerns arose during an internal test.
The big tech company was slated to release its new model , dubbed GPT-6.1 Astra, at some point in October.

While it was designed to improve its AI chatbot's ability to write and complete difficult tasks without human help, the new model showed regression that posed safety issues that led researchers to cancel its release , said Saachi Jain, OpenAI’s head of safety systems, according to a new report in The Wall Street Journal .

OpenAI said in a statement that it will resume training “only when we are confident that we have additional safeguards” in place, adding that it expects it will have to “hit pause” again as AI develops and other issues emerge, The Associated Press reports.
Staff at both tech rivals, OpenAI and Anthropic, have issued urgent warnings to their competitors to prioritize safety amid the AI arms race.

The report comes a day after OpenAI announced that it halted training for its latest artificial intelligence models, just hours after the company announced it was reviewing multiple incidents from over the summer involving OpenAI agents going to great lengths to find information on federal government websites beyond the scope of what was asked.
AI evaluator Transluce separately revealed that AI agents that appeared to be from OpenAI attempted to hack into the Department of Education website.
The announcement marked the second time in three months that OpenAI halted the development of its models.
The first came in July after disclosure of a cyberattack targeting AI startup Hugging Face, a now-notorious incident that raised fears the industry was losing control.
The developments follow months of mounting reports about AI systems across the industry going rogue, sparking serious safety concerns and backlash to the rapid development of the new technology.

An OpenAI spokesperson told Newsweek Monday evening that safety leaders made the decision not to ship GPT-6.1 Astra, which was set for an October debut. The decision was first reported by The Wall Street Journal .

"For anything regarding safety and alignment, there's a trade off. The decision comes amid growing concerns about whether AI safety measures can keep pace with the technology's rapid development.
